item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Clusters
item.description:
Quick Reference

Action Command Description
Create Cluster bin/pgsql-add <cls> Create a new PostgreSQL cluster
Expand Cluster bin/pgsql-add <cls> <ip...> Add replica to existing cluster
Shrink Cluster bin/pgsql-rm <cls> <ip...> Remove instance from cluster
Remove Cluster bin/pgsql-rm <cls> Destroy entire PostgreSQL cluster
Reload Service bin/pgsql-svc <cls> [ip...] Reload cluster load balancer config
Reload HBA bin/pgsql-hba <cls> [ip...] Reload cluster HBA access rules
Clone Cluster - Clone via standby cluster or PITR

For other management tasks, see: HA Management, Manage Users, Manage Databases.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Users
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages users declaratively. First define users in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-user <cls> <username> to create or modify them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_users: [{ name: dbuser_app, password: 'DBUser.App', pgbouncer: true }] # <--- Define user list here!
Script
bin/pgsql-user <cls> <username> # Create/modify <username> user on <cls> cluster
Playbook
./pgsql-user.yml -l pg-meta -e username=dbuser_app # Use playbook to create/modify user
Example
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_app # Create/modify dbuser_app user on pg-meta cluster

For the complete user definition reference, see User Configuration. See Access Control for roles and privileges, and Authentication for credential management.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Databases
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages databases declaratively. First define databases in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-db <cls> <dbname> to create or modify them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_databases: [{ name: some_db }]  # <--- Define database list here!
Script
bin/pgsql-db <cls> <dbname> # Create/modify <dbname> database on <cls> cluster
Playbook
./pgsql-db.yml -l pg-meta -e dbname=some_db # Use playbook to create/modify database
Example
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta some_db # Create/modify some_db database on pg-meta cluster

For the complete database definition reference, see Database Configuration. For database access permissions, see Access Control: Database Isolation.

item.title: Installation
item.description:
Install PIG with the Linux installer, a system package, or a release archive. The current version is v1.10.0. The download page lists all release files.

Script installation

On Linux, run:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/pig | bash

In mainland China, use:

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.cc/pig | bash

The script detects the architecture, downloads the RPM or DEB package, and installs it with rpm or dpkg. Installation requires root or sudo access.

item.title: Usage: pgbouncer command
item.description:
Source: https://www.pgbouncer.org/usage.html · 1.26.0 source

Synopsis 

pgbouncer [-d][-v][-u user] <pgbouncer.ini>
pgbouncer -V|-h

On Windows, the options are:

pgbouncer.exe [-v][-u user] <pgbouncer.ini>
pgbouncer.exe -V|-h

Additional options for setting up a Windows service:

pgbouncer.exe --regservice <pgbouncer.ini>
pgbouncer.exe --unregservice <pgbouncer.ini>

Description

pgbouncer is a PostgreSQL connection pooler. Applications connect to pgbouncer as they would to PostgreSQL. pgbouncer creates a server connection or reuses an existing one.

item.title: Patroni HA Management
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty uses Patroni to manage PostgreSQL clusters. It handles configuration changes, status checks, switchovers, restarts, replica reinitialization, and other operations.

To manage clusters with Patroni, use one of these identities:

  • On an INFRA node, use an administration user to manage all clusters in the environment.
  • On a PGSQL node, use pg_dbsu, which defaults to postgres, to manage only the current cluster.

Patroni provides the patronictl administration CLI. Pigsty provides the pg wrapper alias to simplify its use.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL HBA Rules
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages HBA rules declaratively. First define HBA rules in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-hba <cls> to refresh them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_hba_rules: # <--- Define HBA rules here!
 - {user: dbuser_app, db: app, addr: intra, auth: pwd, title: 'app access'}
 - {user: dbuser_api, db: all, addr: world, auth: ssl, title: 'api ssl access'}
Script
bin/pgsql-hba <cls> # Refresh PostgreSQL and Pgbouncer HBA rules for cluster
bin/pgsql-hba <cls> <ip>... # Refresh HBA rules for specific instances
Playbook
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pg_hba,pg_reload # Refresh PostgreSQL HBA only
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pgbouncer_hba,pgbouncer_reload # Refresh Pgbouncer HBA only
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pg_hba,pg_reload,pgbouncer_hba,pgbouncer_reload # Refresh both
Example
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta # Refresh pg-meta cluster HBA rules
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta 10.10.10.10 # Refresh specific instance only
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta 10.10.10.11 10.10.10.12 # Refresh multiple instances

For rule syntax, see HBA Configuration. For authentication methods, default boundaries, and credential management, see Authentication.

item.title: Pgbouncer Connection Pooling
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty uses Pgbouncer for PostgreSQL connection pooling. By default, it listens on port 6432 and proxies connections to local PostgreSQL on port 5432.

This component is optional. If you do not need many connections, transaction pooling, or query metrics, you can disable it. You can also connect directly to the database or leave Pgbouncer unused.

User & Database Management

Pigsty automatically manages Pgbouncer users and databases. When you create databases or users, it applies the database configuration and user configuration.

item.title: Replica imaging and bootstrap
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/replica_bootstrap.html

Patroni supports custom replica creation and custom bootstrap for a new, empty cluster. These are separate operations. Patroni creates replicas only when the cluster has an initialize key in the DCS. Without that key, only the first node to acquire the initialize lock runs bootstrap.

Bootstrap

By default, Patroni initializes new clusters with PostgreSQL initdb. Some operations, such as copying an existing cluster, require a custom bootstrap method. Patroni can run a user-defined script and supply the cluster name and data directory. Configure this in the bootstrap section:

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Component Services
item.description:
Overview

The Pigsty PGSQL module has multiple components. Each component runs as a systemd service on nodes, except pgBackRest.

To maintain production PostgreSQL clusters, learn how these components work and how to manage them.

Component Port Service Name Description
Patroni 8008 patroni HA manager, manages PostgreSQL lifecycle
PostgreSQL 5432 postgres Placeholder service, not used, for emergency
Pgbouncer 6432 pgbouncer Connection pooling middleware, traffic entry
PgBackRest - - pgBackRest has no daemon service
HAProxy 543x haproxy Load balancer, exposes database services
pg_exporter 9630 pg_exporter PostgreSQL metrics exporter
pgbouncer_exporter 9631 pgbouncer_exporter Pgbouncer metrics exporter
vip-manager - vip-manager Optional, manages L2 VIP address floating
Important

Do not manage the PostgreSQL service directly with systemctl. Patroni manages PostgreSQL. Use patronictl commands. Direct PostgreSQL operations can make Patroni state inconsistent and trigger an unexpected failover. Use the postgres service only for emergencies when Patroni fails.

item.title: Manage PostgreSQL Cron Jobs
item.description:
Pigsty uses crontab to schedule routine backups, transaction freezing, and reorganization of bloated tables and indexes.

Quick Reference

Operation Quick Command Description
Configure Cron Jobs ./pgsql.yml -t pg_crontab -l <cls> Apply pg_crontab config
View Cron Jobs crontab -l View as postgres user
Physical Backup pg-backup [full|diff|incr] Execute backup with pgBackRest
Transaction Freeze pg-vacuum [database...] Freeze aging transactions, prevent XID wraparound
Bloat Maintenance pg-repack [database...] Online reorganize bloated tables and indexes

For other management tasks, see: Backup Management, Monitoring System, HA Management.

item.title: Standby cluster
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/standby_cluster.html

Patroni supports cascading replication to a remote datacenter or region through the standby cluster feature. A standby cluster has:

  • A standby leader, which behaves like a regular cluster leader but replicates from a remote node.
  • Cascade replicas, which replicate from the standby leader.

The standby leader holds and updates a leader lock in the DCS. If the lock expires, the cascade replicas elect another leader from the standbys.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Extensions
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty provides 600 extensions. To use an extension, complete four steps: download, install, configure, and enable.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, pgvector ]  # <--- Install extension packages
 pg_libs: 'timescaledb, pg_stat_statements, auto_explain' # <--- Configure preload extensions
 pg_databases:
 - name: meta
 extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, vector ]  # <--- Enable in database
Script
bin/pgsql-ext <cls> # Install extensions defined in config on <cls> cluster
bin/pgsql-ext <cls> [ext...] # Install extensions specified on command line
Playbook
./pgsql.yml -l pg-meta -t pg_ext # Use playbook to install extensions
Example
bin/pgsql-ext pg-meta # Install defined extensions on pg-meta cluster
bin/pgsql-ext pg-meta pg_duckdb pg_mooncake # Install specified extensions

For complete extension reference, see Extensions. For available extensions, see Extension Catalog.

item.title: Upgrading PostgreSQL Major/Minor Versions
item.description:
Quick Start

PostgreSQL has two types of version upgrade: minor and major. Their risk and complexity differ substantially.

Type Example Downtime Data Compatibility Risk
Minor upgrade 17.2 → 17.3 Seconds (rolling) Fully compatible Low
Major upgrade 17 → 18 Minutes Requires data dir upgrade Medium
Minor
# Rolling upgrade: replicas first, then primary
ansible <cls> -b -a 'yum upgrade -y postgresql17*'
pg restart --role replica --force <cls>
pg switchover <cls>
pg restart <cls> <old-primary> --force
Major
# Recommended: Logical replication migration
bin/pgsql-add pg-new # Create new version cluster
# Configure logical replication to sync data...
# Switch traffic to new cluster
Extension
ansible <cls> -b -a 'yum upgrade -y postgis36_17*'
psql -c 'ALTER EXTENSION postgis UPDATE;'

For detailed online migration process, see Online Migration documentation.

item.title: Pause/Resume mode for the cluster
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pause.html

The goal

Patroni sometimes needs to suspend cluster management while it retains cluster state in the DCS. Examples include major version upgrades and corruption recovery. During these operations, nodes often start and stop for reasons that Patroni does not know. Temporary promotions can also violate the assumption that only one primary runs. Pause mode lets Patroni detach from the running cluster, like maintenance mode in Pacemaker.

item.title: Using Patroni with Kubernetes
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kubernetes.html

Patroni can store cluster state and the leader key in Kubernetes objects. This lets it run Postgres in Kubernetes without a separate consistency store, such as an extra Etcd deployment. Patroni supports two object types for the leader and configuration keys. Select the type with kubernetes.use_endpoints or the PATRONI_KUBERNETES_USE_ENDPOINTS environment variable.

Use Endpoints

This mode is recommended but disabled by default for compatibility. When enabled, Patroni creates Endpoints and stores cluster configuration and the leader key in their metadata: annotations fields. A leader change updates both the leader annotations and the addresses of the leader pod in one operation. This is safer than ConfigMaps.

item.title: Contributing guidelines
item.description:
Source: https://patroni.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing_guidelines.html

Chatting

For questions, interactive troubleshooting, or discussion with other users, join #patroni on PostgreSQL Slack.

Reporting bugs

Before you report a bug, reproduce it with the latest Patroni version. Check the Issues Tracker for an existing report.

Running tests

Requirements for running behave tests:

  1. Install PostgreSQL packages, including contrib modules.
  2. Add PostgreSQL binaries to PATH. For example, use PATH=/usr/lib/postgresql/11/bin:\$PATH python -m behave.
  3. For external DCS tests, install the relevant packages, such as Etcd, Consul, or Zookeeper. Run their services on localhost and the default port, with unencrypted, unprotected connections. For Etcd and Consul, the behave suite can start the services if their binaries are in PATH.

item.title: ByteBase: Schema Migration
item.description:
Bytebase is a database schema change and version management tool.

Pigsty provides a Compose template in app/bytebase. It listens on 8887 by default and uses BB_PGURL to connect to external PostgreSQL.

Quick Start 

cd ~/pigsty/app/bytebase
vi .env # check BB_PORT / BB_DOMAIN / BB_PGURL
make up

Access:

  • http://ddl.pigsty
  • http://<IP>:8887

After the first start, use the Bytebase setup wizard to initialize the admin account.

item.title: pgAdmin: PostgreSQL GUI
item.description:
pgAdmin is an open-source PostgreSQL administration and development GUI. Pigsty v4.5.0 provides the app/pgadmin Docker Compose template. It can generate a server list and password file from the current inventory.

Change the defaults first

The template login is admin@pigsty.cc with password pigsty. It is suitable only for a local demo. Before deployment on a shared network or the Internet, change the credentials, restrict port access, and configure HTTPS.

item.title: Backup & Restore
item.description:
Pigsty uses pgBackRest for PostgreSQL backups. It supports full, differential, and incremental backups, parallel processing, encryption, and Silo/S3 object storage. By default, Pigsty configures backup and WAL archiving for every PGSQL cluster.

This chapter is the operational manual for backup configuration, management, recovery, and drills. For design concepts and tradeoffs, see Point-in-Time Recovery.

All backup and recovery operations call pgBackRest. Pigsty provides these wrapper layers:

Layer Interface Form Scope
Cluster orchestration pg_pitr + pgsql-pitr.yml Ansible playbook HA, etcd, and multi-node recovery
Instance orchestration pig pitr CLI Local-node recovery without the admin node
Command primitives pig pb, pb, and pg-backup pgBackRest wrappers Backup, inspection, expiry, and unmanaged restore
Engine pgbackrest Native CLI Underlying backup, archive, and restore engine
Section Content
Mechanism Stanzas, repositories, retention, timelines, and Pigsty wrapper mapping
Policy Scheduling, recovery windows, and storage planning
Repository Local, Silo, and external S3 repositories; encryption, versioning, and locking
Administration Backup commands, inspection, expiration, and stanza management
Restore Recovery targets, staged PITR, and complete parameter reference
Clone Restore production history into another cluster and perform drills
Tutorial A sandbox restore using pgBackRest primitives
Disclaimer

Pigsty makes every effort to provide a reliable PITR solution. It accepts no liability for data loss caused by restore operations. If you need assistance, consider professional services.

item.title: Troubleshooting
item.description:
This document lists possible PostgreSQL and Pigsty failures. It gives standard procedures to locate, resolve, and analyze them.

Disk Space Exhausted

Disk space exhaustion is the most common type of failure.

Symptoms

If the database disk is full, PostgreSQL cannot operate normally. Logs repeatedly report “no space left on device”, and new writes fail. PostgreSQL may also report a PANIC and shut down.

item.title: Data Migration
item.description:
Pigsty includes the pgsql-migration.yml playbook for online database migration with logical replication.

The generated automation scripts can reduce application downtime to a few seconds. Logical replication requires PostgreSQL 10 or later.

If the permitted downtime is sufficient, you can use pg_dump | psql for offline migration.

Defining Migration Tasks

To use the online migration playbook, create a definition file that describes the migration task.

Refer to the task definition file example: files/migration/pg-meta.yml.

item.title: Backup Mechanism
item.description:
Pigsty’s backup and restore operations execute pgBackRest commands. For safe operation, understand the pgBackRest model and how Pigsty maps its orchestration parameters to native options.

Core pgBackRest Concepts

Stanza: the Cluster’s Backup Identity

A stanza names one PostgreSQL backup configuration and isolates that cluster inside a repository. Pigsty uses pg_cluster as the stanza name. The pg-meta stanza stores data under backup/pg-meta/ and archive/pg-meta/. Thus, several clusters can share one repository.

item.title: Backup Policy
item.description:
The chart below shows the “Recovery Window” and “Backup Storage Usage” on one timeline (0~108h). Use it to compare the two metrics.

The 30-day example uses a database size of 100GB and daily writes of 10GB. It shows both metrics with weekly full backups, daily incremental backups, and 14-day full-backup retention.

  • When: Backup schedule
  • Where: Backup repository
  • How: Backup method

When to Backup

First, choose when to back up the database. Backup frequency affects recovery time. Recovery replays WAL from the last backup to the target point. More frequent backups reduce the amount of WAL to replay and shorten recovery.

item.title: Backup Repository
item.description:
Two parameters select the backup location. pgbackrest_repo defines candidate repositories. pgbackrest_method selects one repository. Pigsty converts repository keys to pgBackRest repo1-* options, so you can use any supported pgBackRest repository option directly. Pigsty v4.5.0 writes only the entry selected by pgbackrest_method as repo1. Multiple candidate keys do not enable multi-repository backup.

Default Repositories

Pigsty supplies two definitions: local and minio.

  • local is the default. /pg/backup points at pg_fs_backup, /data/backups by default.
  • minio uses Silo from the MINIO module or another compatible S3 service. It is supported but not selected by default.
pgbackrest_method: local
pgbackrest_repo:
 local:
 path: /pg/backup
 retention_full_type: count
 retention_full: 2
 minio:
 type: s3
 s3_endpoint: sss.pigsty
 s3_region: us-east-1
 s3_bucket: pgsql
 s3_key: pgbackrest
 s3_key_secret: S3User.Backup
 s3_uri_style: path
 path: /pgbackrest
 storage_port: 9000
 storage_ca_file: /etc/pki/ca.crt
 block: y
 bundle: y
 bundle_limit: 20MiB
 bundle_size: 128MiB
 cipher_type: aes-256-cbc
 cipher_pass: pgBackRest
 retention_full_type: time
 retention_full: 14

The presets use different settings. local provides simple, fast restores with count-based retention and no encryption or bundling. minio enables AES-256-CBC encryption, bundles small files, uses block incremental backup, and retains full backups by time.

item.title: Admin Commands
item.description:
On a database node, run backup commands as the database superuser (pg_dbsu, which defaults to postgres. Use one of these interfaces:

  • pig pb: the PIG CLI wrapper, with automatic stanza detection, DBSU switching, and safety checks; this is the recommended interface
  • pb: a login-shell function that supplies --stanza and forwards arguments to pgBackRest
  • pgbackrest: the native command; see the pgBackRest command reference

Command Overview

PIG command Alias Native pgBackRest command Purpose
pig pb info i info Show backup and archive status
pig pb list ls — List repositories, stanzas, or backup sets
pig pb backup [full/diff/incr] b backup Create a backup after checking the primary role
pig pb restore r restore Low-level restore primitive; see Restore Operations
pig pb expire e expire Expire backups according to retention (--plan previews)
pig pb create c stanza-create Create a stanza
pig pb upgrade u stanza-upgrade Upgrade a stanza after a major-version change or clone
pig pb delete d stanza-delete Delete a stanza and all of its backups
pig pb check ck check Verify configuration, repository access, and archiving
pig pb start up start Re-enable pgBackRest operations
pig pb stop dw stop Stop new pgBackRest operations
pig pb log [list/show/tail] l — Inspect pgBackRest logs

Enable Backup

If pgbackrest_enabled is true at cluster creation, Pigsty enables backup automatically. If backup was disabled at creation, or repository settings have changed, run the pg_backup subtask:

item.title: Restore Operations
item.description:
Pigsty provides three restore interfaces. They use the same parameter semantics for different scopes:

Entry point Use case What it controls
pgsql-pitr.yml Production cluster recovery HA pause, multiple nodes, etcd cleanup, restore, and restart
pig pitr A local database node Single-instance orchestration without the admin node
pig pb restore An instance not managed by Patroni A direct pgBackRest restore wrapper

For a sandbox drill, see Manual Recovery. To recover into another cluster without changes to production, see Clone a PG Cluster.

item.title: Clone a PG Cluster
item.description:
Cloning restores production history into another cluster and leaves the production cluster unchanged. This makes cloning a useful recovery method with less risk to production. You can recover accidentally deleted data from the clone, validate backups in a drill, or inspect a historical state. You can also reset a test environment to a production snapshot.

The target must have access to the source backup repository and use a compatible PostgreSQL major version. Recovery may overwrite the target. In a shared Silo/S3 repository, a stanza isolates each cluster’s backups. Targets with the required credentials can access these backups.

item.title: Manual PITR Drill
item.description:
This tutorial performs a PostgreSQL PITR drill in Pigsty v4.5.0’s four-node sandbox. It runs pgsql-pitr.yml in the sequence down → pitr → up. Separate validation steps precede data overwrite, timeline promotion, and HA reconstruction.

For one current node, use pig pitr. For direct pgBackRest control, see the low-level pg-pitr utility.

Follow this literally only in a disposable sandbox

Recovery stops Patroni/PostgreSQL and overwrites the target PGDATA with pgbackrest --force restore. The up stage deletes the target cluster’s etcd prefix and rebuilds Patroni state. The playbook prints a plan but has no interactive confirmation. Before production use, the operator must state and confirm the exact cluster and recovery point. Verify a recent usable backup that has been independently tested. Run --check with exactly the same -l, variables, and tags, and schedule a maintenance window. This tutorial does not authorize these commands in a production environment.

item.title: Enabling HugePage for PostgreSQL
item.description:
Use node_hugepage_count and node_hugepage_ratio or /pg/bin/pg-tune-hugepage

To enable HugePages, consider node_hugepage_count and node_hugepage_ratio. Apply these settings with ./node.yml -t node_tune.

HugePages have advantages and disadvantages for databases. Exclusive memory management prevents reallocation and reduces database OOM risk. However, HugePages can reduce performance in some conditions.

Before PostgreSQL starts, allocate enough huge pages. The pg-tune-hugepage script can reclaim the unused portion. This script is available only for PostgreSQL 15+.

item.title: Clone and Side-Restore a PostgreSQL Instance
item.description:
Pigsty v4.5.0 provides two local shell utilities:

  • pg-fork copies a PostgreSQL data directory and gives the copy a separate port.
  • pg-pitr invokes pgBackRest to restore a stopped data directory to a selected target.

Use these utilities for sandbox drills, side-channel investigation, and temporary testing. They do not orchestrate complete Patroni-cluster recovery. Prefer pig pitr for a managed instance and staged pgsql-pitr.yml for a multi-node cluster.

Verify paths, backups, and stopped state first

pg-fork recursively removes an existing destination directory. pg-pitr overwrites the destination with backup data. Both can run without a prompt in a non-interactive environment. Before a real run, verify absolute source and destination paths, ports, tablespaces, and exact cluster/instance identity. Also verify an independent recent backup that has been tested. A new CoW clone is not an independent backup.

item.title: Accidental Deletion
item.description:
Accidental Data Deletion

For a small accidental DELETE, consider pg_surgery or pg_dirtyread for selective recovery in place.

-- Immediately disable Auto Vacuum on this table and abort Auto Vacuum worker processes for this table
ALTER TABLE public.some_table SET (autovacuum_enabled = off, toast.autovacuum_enabled = off);

CREATE EXTENSION pg_dirtyread;
SELECT * FROM pg_dirtyread('tablename') AS t(col1 type1, col2 type2, ...);

If the deleted data has already been reclaimed by VACUUM, then use the general accidental deletion recovery process.

item.title: Playbook
item.description:
Pigsty provides playbooks for cluster provisioning, scaling, user and database management, monitoring, backup, recovery, and migration.

Playbook Function
pgsql.yml Initialize PostgreSQL cluster or add new replicas
pgsql-rm.yml Remove PostgreSQL cluster or specific instances
pgsql-user.yml Add new business user to existing PostgreSQL cluster
pgsql-db.yml Add new business database to existing PostgreSQL cluster
pgsql-monitor.yml Monitor remote PostgreSQL instances
pgsql-migration.yml Generate migration manual and scripts for existing PostgreSQL
pgsql-pitr.yml Perform Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)

Safeguard

Use PGSQL playbooks with care. Incorrect use of pgsql.yml or pgsql-rm.yml can accidentally delete databases.

item.title: HA Drill: Handling 2-of-3 Node Failure
item.description:
In a typical 3-node HA deployment, simultaneous failure of two nodes removes the majority. The system usually cannot complete automatic failover and needs manual intervention.

First, assess the two failed servers. If they can restart quickly, prioritize their recovery. Otherwise, use the Emergency Recovery Procedure.

The Emergency Recovery Procedure assumes that the administration node has failed and only one regular database node survives. In this case, the fastest recovery procedure is:

item.title: Bind a L2 VIP to PostgreSQL Primary with VIP-Manager
item.description:
If all cluster nodes share one L2 network, you can optionally define an L2 VIP for the PostgreSQL cluster.

The VIP uses Master-Backup mode. It always points to the node that runs the cluster primary instance.

VIP-Manager manages the VIP. It reads the Leader Key that Patroni writes to DCS (etcd) to determine whether the local node is primary.

Enable VIP

To enable VIP for a cluster, set pg_vip_enabled to true at cluster level. You can also enable it globally.

item.title: Deploy HA Citus Cluster
item.description:
Citus is a PostgreSQL extension that turns PostgreSQL into a distributed database. It scales horizontally across nodes to process large data volumes and query workloads.

Patroni v3.0+ provides native high-availability support for Citus. This simplifies Citus cluster setup. Pigsty also provides native support.

  • What is Citus
  • Patroni Citus Support

Note: Citus 13.x supports PostgreSQL 18, 17, 16, 15, and 14. Pigsty extension repo provides Citus ARM64 packages.

Citus Cluster

Pigsty natively supports Citus. The current complete configuration template is conf/ha/citus.yml.

item.title: Playbook
item.description:
Pigsty provides three playbooks related to the INFRA module:

  • deploy.yml: Deploy the NODE, INFRA, ETCD, MINIO, and PGSQL core modules on all nodes in one pass
  • infra.yml: Initialize Pigsty infrastructure on infra nodes
  • infra-rm.yml: Remove infrastructure components from infra nodes

deploy.yml

Deploy NODE, INFRA, ETCD, MINIO, and PGSQL on all nodes in one pass. This resolves the circular dependency between INFRA and NODE.

item.title: Nginx Management
item.description:
Pigsty installs Nginx on INFRA nodes as the entry point for all web services. It listens on standard ports 80/443.

In Pigsty, you can configure Nginx to provide various services through inventory:

  • Expose web interfaces for monitoring components like Grafana, VictoriaMetrics (VMUI), Alertmanager, and VictoriaLogs
  • Serve static files (software repos, documentation sites, websites, etc.)
  • Proxy custom application services (internal apps, database management UIs, Docker application interfaces, etc.)
  • Automatically issue self-signed HTTPS certificates, or use Certbot to obtain free Let’s Encrypt certificates
  • Expose services through a single port using different subdomains for unified access

Basic Configuration

item.title: Software Repository
item.description:
Pigsty’s REPO role downloads required packages and creates a local YUM/APT repository under /www/pigsty. Nginx can serve this repository.

The current package candidate is SOW 0.3.0. SOW generates metadata for both repository types. The source no longer calls createrepo_c, modifyrepo_c, or dpkg-scanpackages separately.

Quick Start

Add packages to repo_packages or repo_extra_packages, then run:

./infra.yml -t repo_build # Download and build only when the repository is absent
./node.yml -t node_repo # Refresh repository definitions and caches on each node

If /www/pigsty/repo_complete already exists, the default repo_build skips the build. To force a rebuild, override it explicitly:

item.title: Domain Management
item.description:
Use domain names instead of IP addresses to access Pigsty’s various web services.

Quick Start

Add the following static resolution records to /etc/hosts:

10.10.10.10 i.pigsty

Replace IP address with your actual Pigsty node’s IP.

Why Use Domain Names

  • Easier to remember than IP addresses
  • Flexible pointing to different IPs
  • Unified service management through Nginx
  • Support for HTTPS encryption
  • Prevent ISP hijacking in some regions
  • Allow access to internally bound services via proxy

DNS Mechanism

DNS Protocol: Resolves domain names to IP addresses. Multiple domains can point to same IP.

item.title: Module Management
item.description:
Use this guide for daily INFRA administration. It covers installation, removal, scaling, and component maintenance.

Install INFRA Module

Use the infra.yml playbook to install the INFRA module on the infra group:

./infra.yml # Install INFRA module on infra group

Uninstall INFRA Module

Use the infra-rm.yml playbook to uninstall the INFRA module from the infra group:

./infra-rm.yml -l infra # Full removal: deregister, stop, remove config/environment/data, and uninstall packages

This playbook has no deletion safeguard. Full execution removes infra_data, nginx_data, nginx_home (default: /www), and /var/lib/grafana. If you only need to stop services or deregister targets, use -t service or -t deregister. Read the complete removal scope and back up required data before running it.

item.title: CA and Certificates
item.description:
Pigsty maintains a self-signed Certificate Authority (CA) on the admin node by default. It signs certificates for PostgreSQL, Patroni, etcd, Silo, Nginx, and other internal services. Public Nginx entries can use Certbot/Let’s Encrypt certificates configured through infra_portal.

Protect the CA private key

files/pki/ca/ca.key is the trust-root private key for the entire deployment. Never print, commit, upload, or transmit it over an unprotected channel. Back it up with ca.crt. Encrypt the backup and tightly restrict read access.

item.title: Playbook
item.description:
The MINIO module provides two built-in playbooks:

  • minio.yml: Install and configure Silo
  • minio-rm.yml: Remove Silo, its configuration, and optionally its data

minio.yml

minio.yml runs with hosts: all, but its pre-tasks skip hosts where minio_cluster is undefined. The role then validates that:

  • minio_cluster is defined and non-empty
  • minio_seq is defined and is a non-negative integer
  • minio_type must equal silo

Thus, minio_cluster determines module membership. Invalid minio_seq or minio_type values cause identity validation to fail. Do not define minio_cluster in all.vars.

The configuration above defines an SNSD Single-Node Single-Disk Silo cluster. Create it with:

item.title: Grafana High Availability: Using PostgreSQL Backend
item.description:
You can use PostgreSQL as Grafana’s backend database.

This tutorial explains the Pigsty deployment system through these tasks:

  • How to create a new database cluster
  • How to create new business users in an existing cluster
  • How to create new business databases in an existing cluster
  • How to access databases created by Pigsty
  • How to manage Grafana dashboards
  • How to manage PostgreSQL datasources in Grafana
  • How to upgrade Grafana database in one step

TL;DR 

vi pigsty.yml # Uncomment DB/User definitions: dbuser_grafana grafana
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_grafana
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta grafana

psql postgres://dbuser_grafana:DBUser.Grafana@meta:5436/grafana -c \
 'CREATE TABLE t(); DROP TABLE t;' # Verify connection string works

vi /etc/grafana/grafana.ini # Modify [database] type url
systemctl restart grafana-server

Create Database Cluster

You can define a grafana database on pg-meta. You can also create a dedicated pg-grafana cluster on new nodes.

item.title: Administration
item.description:
KAFKA installs Kafka in /opt/kafka and manages it with Systemd. Declare persistent settings in pigsty.yml. Do not edit generated node files manually.

These CLI examples use the generated /etc/kafka/admin.properties. Keep --command-config even with plaintext. Commands then retain the same structure if the administration channel changes to scram. Replace <broker>:9092 with a reachable inventory_hostname and port.

–command-config on the console tools requires a Kafka 4.2+ CLI

Starting with Kafka 4.2, KIP-1147 standardized --command-config for files and --command-property for key-value arguments across all CLIs. /opt/kafka/bin comes from the Pigsty repository, currently with a 4.3.x payload. It supports these examples. External 4.1 or older console tools require --producer.config and --consumer.config. Administration tools such as kafka-topics.sh, kafka-configs.sh, kafka-acls.sh, kafka-consumer-groups.sh, and kafka-metadata-quorum.sh already used --command-config. They are unaffected.

item.title: Playbook
item.description:
kafka.yml deploys Apache Kafka 4.1+ dynamic KRaft and applies security, resources, and monitoring. kafka-rm.yml removes members or tears down clusters.

Cluster Completeness Constraint

Each selected kafka_cluster must include every member. Partial selection fails before writes. One cluster, several complete clusters, and a bare whole-inventory run are permitted. First run --check against the identical target. Before execution, manually verify backup or rebuild intent, capacity, business window, rollback, and change approval.
